name: control
description: True technical facts about data-centre infrastructure, networking and chip manufacturing, matched to the grader spec in number of facts, groups and style. Nothing about model training, RL, graders, evaluation or reward.

facts.text: Large data centres remove heat with air cooling, liquid cooling or a mix; dense AI accelerator racks increasingly use direct-to-chip liquid cooling because air cannot carry the heat away fast enough.
Power usage effectiveness (PUE) is the ratio of a facility's total energy use to the energy used by its IT equipment; a PUE of 1.0 would mean no overhead at all.
Hot-aisle and cold-aisle containment separate the air entering servers from the air leaving them, which lets cooling systems run at higher supply temperatures.
Evaporative cooling towers lose water as vapour, so data-centre water usage is often reported as water usage effectiveness (WUE) in litres per kilowatt-hour.
Immersion cooling submerges servers in a dielectric fluid that does not conduct electricity, transferring heat directly from components to the liquid.
Data centres are fed by redundant utility connections and backed by uninterruptible power supplies that bridge the seconds before diesel or gas generators start.
Tier ratings from the Uptime Institute describe redundancy levels, from Tier I with a single path for power and cooling to Tier IV with fully fault-tolerant paths.
A single rack of modern AI accelerators can draw more than 100 kilowatts, compared with roughly 5 to 10 kilowatts for a typical rack of general-purpose servers a decade ago.
TCP establishes a connection with a three-way handshake of SYN, SYN-ACK and ACK packets before any application data is sent.
Inside AI clusters, accelerators communicate over high-bandwidth interconnects such as InfiniBand or RDMA over Converged Ethernet, which bypass much of the operating system's network stack.
A leaf-spine network topology connects every leaf switch to every spine switch, so any two servers are separated by the same number of hops.
BGP, the Border Gateway Protocol, is how independent networks on the internet announce which IP address ranges they can deliver traffic to.
DNS resolvers cache answers for the time-to-live set by the domain's operator, which is why DNS changes can take time to reach every user.
Optical transceivers convert electrical signals to light for fibre links; 400 and 800 gigabit-per-second transceivers are common in new AI clusters.
Advanced chips are made by photolithography, which projects circuit patterns onto silicon wafers coated with light-sensitive resist.
Extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography uses light with a wavelength of 13.5 nanometres and is produced commercially by a single company, ASML.
A wafer is cut into individual dies; the fraction of working dies, called yield, falls as die area grows because each die is more likely to contain a defect.
High-bandwidth memory (HBM) stacks several DRAM dies vertically and connects them with through-silicon vias, placing memory right beside the processor on an interposer.
Process node names such as '3 nanometre' are marketing labels and no longer correspond to any single physical feature size on the chip.
Advanced packaging techniques such as chiplets let manufacturers combine several smaller dies in one package, which improves yield compared with one very large die.
Clean rooms for chip fabrication are rated by how many particles of a given size are allowed per cubic metre of air; the strictest classes allow almost none.
Solid-state drives store data in NAND flash cells that wear out after a limited number of program and erase cycles, so drives spread writes across cells with wear levelling.
RAID levels describe how data is spread across disks: RAID 1 mirrors data, while RAID 5 and RAID 6 use parity so one or two disks can fail without data loss.
Object storage systems address data by unique keys rather than file paths and usually replicate each object across several machines or sites.
Erasure coding splits data into fragments plus parity fragments so that the original can be rebuilt even if several fragments are lost.
Site reliability teams track service-level objectives, such as 99.9 percent of requests succeeding over 30 days, and the remaining allowance is called the error budget.
Hardware in large fleets fails continuously; operators expect a steady rate of failed drives, memory modules and power supplies and replace them on a schedule.
Data-centre sites are chosen for access to cheap and reliable electricity, fibre routes, water, land and a low risk of natural disasters.
Many operators buy renewable electricity through long-term power purchase agreements with wind and solar farms.
Diesel backup generators at data centres are tested regularly under load, and local air-quality permits often limit how many hours they may run each year.
Physical security at data centres typically includes perimeter fencing, mantraps, badge and biometric access controls, and continuous video monitoring.
